title: The Kav: how a line comes out of the point, a hiyuli that only makes an up and a down
overview:
Chapter 14 turns to the *Kav*, the line drawn from the *reshimu*, and first asks a general question. The *reshimu* is a point. The *tzimtzum* is no obstacle, since the whole infinite light was stuffed into that point, as a blueprint holds a whole house. But a point does not spread out at all: practically it seems a true *tzimtzum*, like one word that means all of Shakespeare. So how can a line, its very opposite, come out of it?

The answer is that the point is a *hiyuli*. Like clay, letters, or the ground without a seed, it does not spread out because it could become anything, not because it is held back. Points joined make a line, as a teacher breaks "math" into subjects, and a good student is a point only while he absorbs. The first line is short: it only makes an up and a down, one standard of measure like a single ruler for the whole house, and so it is called the *kav hamida*. Yet it carries the real light of the Essence, measured to the receivers.

blocks.text:
And now: the light before the *tzimtzum* (contraction) was explained, and the *tzimtzum* and the *reshimu* (the impression left after it). Now comes the next stage in the *hishtalshelus* (the chain of descent): the *Kav* and the *chut*, the line and the thread, which comes out from this *reshimu*. And as it was said that everything is going to be explained in detail, this too has to be understood in detail.

But first, before getting into the details of the *Kav* and *chut*, it has to be understood in general. There is a general question about the *Kav*: generally speaking, the *Kav* is the exact opposite of the *reshimu*.

phrases.he: כי הנה הנקודה מורה ההעלם והסתלקות הכל, עד שלא נשאר רק כנקודה א'
phrases.en: All of the light, the whole infinite light, was all hidden, and all that was left was one point.

phrases.en: Also, this tiny little point that's left of everything that was there before is in a way that it doesn't spread out, because it's a point.

phrases.en: It has no *hispashtus*, which means it doesn't have an *orech*, it doesn't have a *rochav*.

phrases.en: It's just a point, has no inside.

blocks.text: What was the point? All of the light, the whole infinite light of everything that G-d could do and be, even all the fishes He can create and all the infinite flavors of bubble gum, all of it was hidden, and all that was left was one point. And even this one tiny little point, left of everything that was there before, is in a way that it does not spread out, because it is a point. That too shows that it does not come out.

An important thing, which may have been said before: relative to the *Ein Sof* (the Infinite) and everything before the *tzimtzum*, the *reshimu* is like a zero. All the light is hidden in it; it is like a nothing. But compared to everything that comes out afterwards, it is completely infinite.

It has no *hispashtus* (spreading forth) at all, which means it has no *orech* (length) and no *rochav* (breadth). It is just a point, with nothing in the middle; it does not go out long or wide. It looks like the letter yud. How do you write a yud? It is just a point and has no inside, while all the other letters have more dimensions to them.

sections.title: The tzimtzum is no obstacle: everything was put into the point
sections.summary: The *tzimtzum* did not take the light away but stuffed all of it into the point, as a blueprint holds the whole house. So, on the contrary, the *reshimu* is the source of every revelation that comes after it.

phrases.he: דהיינו מה שנשאר בבחינת נקודה לבד,
phrases.en: which is that all the light was hidden in just one point,
It could be the opposite, it could be that there would be a revelation coming out from the *reshimu*.

blocks.text: Now we are going to see what the real problem of this *reshimu* is: why does it seem unable to be revealed? It is not the *tzimtzum*, the kind that leaves only a point, where all the light was hidden in just one point. The last two chapters explained that the light was not actually removed completely, which would mean the *tzimtzum* *kipshuto* (literally). It was not removed; it was hidden in a point.

blocks.title: The blueprint, the thrown stone and the peace sign
blocks.text: Like the blueprint, which has the whole building in it, or the sign to remember something, which has the whole intellect in it: totally hidden, and yet it is all there. When you throw a stone, your whole power of movement is hidden in the stone, and even your whole essence, which is why, if it kills somebody, they will kill you, G-d save us. Or the hand motion that hints at a very deep intellect, like a peace sign for the hippies: it hints at their whole philosophy, but it is really just two fingers. You see no intellect there, and yet the whole intellect is hidden there. And writing: you see no intellect in fingers twitching. Even the person writing does not consciously see the *sechel* (intellect) there; he sees only his fingers moving, and yet it all comes through onto the paper. The whole essence is there too.

So the *tzimtzum* is not a problem, because it is all there. If the *tzimtzum* had taken away all the light, there would be a question how it could be revealed again. But it did not take it all away; it put it all in there. On the contrary, that is why the *reshimu* can be the source of everything that comes afterwards: it was all stuffed in there, so whatever you want to bring out, it is there. The whole *koach* (power) of the *Ein Sof*, the whole infinite light: every flavor of bubble gum, the last one, every song, every sight, every flavor, everything. So as far as the *tzimtzum* that leaves only a *nekuda* (a point) goes, it could be the opposite: there could be a revelation coming out from the *reshimu*.

phrases.he: מפני שמחמת זה יוכלל בו הכל
phrases.en: because since it had this type of a *tzimtzum*, everything was put into it.
just that it's in a very short and hinted way,
on the contrary,

phrases.he: זהו עיקר סיבת כל גלוי ההשפעה כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: Because the *tzimtzum* was of this kind, everything was put into the point. It is true that it made it into a point, but it made it into a point because it stuffed everything in; the whole infinity was put there. Only it is there **in a very short and hinted way**, like the analogies said before of the mnemonic and the signs to remember.

**On the contrary**, this is the main cause of all the revelation. All the lights in the *hishtalshelus* come out from the *reshimu*; they are re-extracted from it again. It is like what was said about the *Mishna*, how the original *Gemara* was reconstituted from it: the *Mishna* took the *Gemara* and put it down into a short form, and from there the whole thing was reconstituted.

blocks.title: Frank Lloyd Wright's few notes
blocks.text: Or a blueprint: the whole plan of how to build a house. "What's this guy's name, the famous... Frank Lloyd Wright?" He puts down a few notes and makes a little drawing, and the whole house comes out of it. It is all there, in a hidden way, and that is why it is all able to come out. The same is true of all the other analogies.

blocks.title: A tool shed instead of Fallingwater
blocks.text: What would be *tzimtzum kipshuto*, where things could not come out? Say they hired him to make Fallingwater, and while he is making the blueprint he decides: "Nah, I don't want to make them a beautiful, artistic building with all my architectural ability and know-how. Instead, I'm going to write them a blueprint for a little tool shed." Not over the waterfall; just a little shack in the woods. There he actually left out a lot. Or if he said, "You know what? I'm not even going to do it at all": that would be complete *tzimtzum*, *kipshuto*. They say, "Would you build us a thing? We'll pay you a lot of money," and he says, "No, sorry, won't do it." He is holding back his wisdom. So there is partial and complete *tzimtzum* in that way, and that is *kipshuto*. Here nothing is lost; it is all just put in a hidden way.
This *tzimtzum*, the fact that everything was put into the point, is the whole reason why there could be the whole *gilui* (revelation) afterwards: because it is all there.

blocks.title: The builders and the blueprint
blocks.text: How do they build the house? Frank Lloyd Wright did not go there and build it and tell them what to do the whole time. So how did they know? The builders are not necessarily very smart: "They could just be these stupid people that don't know very much. You know, they know how to bang in a nail and drill in a screw." They have to learn whatever they have to learn, but they do not have to be artistic or know engineering, all the things Frank Lloyd Wright had to know. They can be simple people who know how to build, which is also a *chachma* (wisdom), but a *chachma* of the hands instead of an artistic one, or a brain *chachma* like engineering.

The builders do not need to know what he knew: they know how to bang in a nail and drill in a screw. They have to learn whatever they have to learn, but they do not have to be artistic or know engineering, all the things Frank Lloyd Wright had to know. They can be simple people who know how to build, which is also a *chachma* (wisdom), but a *chachma* of the hands instead of an artistic one, or a brain *chachma* like engineering.

blocks.title: Whose house is it?
blocks.text: So how did they do it? In fact they did better than Frank Lloyd Wright. He just drew it on paper; they actually built it. It is not so hard to draw a nice house on paper; it is a lot harder to build one. They made the *chiddush* (the new thing). Nobody makes a big deal about the drawing; people make a big deal about the house. So why do we even say it is his house, that he made it? He did not touch one brick of it. Because the whole reason the house came out revealed in that shape is that they were following the blueprint he made, into which he put his whole wisdom of how to make the house. So it is his house, and his *etzem* (essence) gets connected to it: if it had fallen down, they would have sued him for not being an engineer. He could have made any house he wanted; the *mashal* (analogy) just takes this one.

The *mashal* is that all of his wisdom and knowledge of how to make this house he puts into the blueprint, and then you do not need him anymore. If you want to change something, you need him again, to make a new one. To change even one line on it, one little thing, you have to get him to come back and look it over, because only he understands what everything is for and how it all works together. They do not know.

blocks.title: The palace that collapsed for one dot
blocks.text:
You know the story of the architect who made plans for a king, for a palace. Whether it was left out when it was copied over, or the builder just did not care, there was one dot on the plan that they forgot to build. But that dot stood for the central support beam that went through the whole structure. From a bird's eye view on the blueprint it was just one dot, not the main thing like the walls. They left it out, built the whole thing, and it collapsed. Why? Because they left out this one little dot. "It's just a little thing. It's a little dot. I did the main thing." But if you are missing the central point that holds it all up, it does not matter how little it is. The builders do not have to know or understand why it is important.

The blueprint is like the *reshimu*. The dot is not: it is like the *reshimu* because it is a dot, but that is not what is being talked about here.

sections.title: Yet the point does not spread out: how can a line come from it?
sections.summary: Practically, what is hidden in one point is not there for us, like a single word meaning all of Shakespeare, or a black hole. The beginning of the answer: a point and a line are not two opposites, because points joined together make a line.

phrases.he: אבל מה שמנקודה זו מורה העדר ההתפשטות לגמרי למטה
phrases.en: but since this point is in a way that it totally doesn't spread out to below,

phrases.he: לכאורה, זהו ודאי נקרא צמצום גמור ואמיתי
phrases.en: seemingly, this is a complete and true *tzimtzum*,

phrases.he: להעלים ולהסתיר לבלתי יבוא האור למטה

blocks.text: So as far as the *tzimtzum* goes, it seems there is no problem having a *gilui* come afterwards. But this point is in a way that it totally does not spread out to below; it is all stuffed into a point. Seemingly, then, this is a complete and true *tzimtzum*: the light is being concealed and covered over so that it should not come below. It is not being given over to those below; it is being hidden from them.

blocks.title: A string around your finger, and Roy G. Biv
blocks.text: Say you put something in code: you took the intellect and hid it in such a way that it is all there, but nobody is ever going to get it. Instead of a blueprint, since the *reshimu* is even shorter than a blueprint, he puts it all into one dot. Nobody will figure out how to make the building from one dot. In his own mind it reminds him of everything, like a string around your finger, but someone else sees no *sechel* there. Or a mnemonic: "My very eager mother served us nine juicy pickles," or something like that. You would never figure out that it is a mnemonic for the order of the planets unless you were told; it is too short, and you cannot see the connection. And that is not even a total point yet. It can be shorter, like Roy G. Biv for the order of the colors of the rainbow. And then it gets so short that it is just one point, and you are never going to figure it out.

The *reshimu* has two aspects. On the one hand, everything is there: that is the whole point of the last few chapters, that the *tzimtzum* is not *kipshuto* but puts everything into the *reshimu*. And yet it is hidden completely. As far as the first aspect goes there is no problem, because everything is there. But as far as the second goes, it is all hidden: even though it is all there, practically, for me, it is not there. "I don't care if it's there, you know?"

blocks.title: One word for all of Shakespeare, and "math" on the board
blocks.text: Say we make a language, and instead of a word for one thing (some languages have one word for what another says in a few), we make one word that means all of the Shakespearean plays. You are never going to figure it out. Or the teacher walks into class, writes "math" on the board, and says, "That word has it all in it. Everything that you're going to learn in this class, and in the next class, all your years in school learning this subject, it's all included in this one word. Learn it well and you'll know everything you have to know." And he walks out and leaves them there. They are never going to figure anything out. It is true that it is all in there, but it is put down to one point, so there is no way for them to get it out. It is hidden.

So it seems the *tzimtzum* is still *kipshuto*. In a way it was not total, because He was not hiding the light, only contracting it and stuffing it into this point. But as far as we are concerned, He is intentionally hiding it from us, by making it so short that we are never going to figure it out.

blocks.title: Parents speaking another language
blocks.text: Sometimes two people do not want others to understand: parents talk to each other in a different language so their kids will not understand. They are saying everything, but for the kids it is as if they are not saying it. Or two scientists speak in jargon that normal people will not understand: they are saying everything, but to regular people it is totally hidden, because it is put in a way they do not know.

blocks.title: Why the Zohar was written so hidden
blocks.text:
Or as it says about the *Zohar*: Rabbi Chaim Vital writes in his introduction to *Etz Chaim* (the Arizal's Tree of Life) that the wisdom of the *Zohar* was really supposed to be hidden. It was not allowed to be revealed then; only right before *Moshiach* comes is it allowed to be revealed. So why was he allowed to write it? Because he wrote it in such a way, so hidden, that it is as if it was not written. And if you open up the *Zohar* and try to read it, even with commentaries, it is so hidden that it is as if he did not write it, until now. Now we are starting to open it up.

So why did he write it at all? What's the point? The whole reason the *Zohar* was written, he answers, is that right before *Moshiach* comes they will learn how to open up these wisdoms and know what they mean. It was written really for them. And now we are at that time, when we are able to start opening it up and pulling it out. All the Kabbala and the secrets of the Torah and *Chassidus* (Chassidic teaching) are really written for us.

phrases.en: if so, that it's totally in a way of a point,
How does the *Kav* come out from the *reshimu*?
the *Kav* is the opposite of this,

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת המשכה והתפשטות דקו כו'.
phrases.en: that *Kav* means a revelation and *hispashtus*.

blocks.text: If so, that it is totally in the way of a point, how can its very opposite be drawn from it? The *Kav* means *hamshacha* (drawing down) and *hispashtus*, a revelation and a spreading out. How does the *Kav* come out from the *reshimu*? It seems the *reshimu* is a complete *tzimtzum* for the *Kav* and lets nothing out. Even though it is all there, it is not letting it out.

blocks.title: Worse than a black hole
blocks.text: It seems like a black hole that just sucks everything in. You say, "Oh, we'll go with a spaceship and pull out some stuff," and they just get sucked in, and the more they try to get out, the more they get sucked in. That is the power of the *reshimu*, the power of *tzimtzum*: the infinite power of *gevura* (might, restraint) to take everything and condense it all into one point. Even more than a black hole, because a black hole has some size. Take our whole solar system and make it into a black hole, and it would be the size of a bowling ball. Compared to what it was that is very small, since the earth is huge and the sun is way bigger, but it is already a pretty big size. G-d can make an infinitely small point and put everything into it.
And that is all just the physical. This is much more than the physical: the whole physical world is like nothing. "The whole physical world is just made from angel poop, you know."

sensitivity.reason: Calls the physical world "angel poop", a crude image.
sensitivity.publishable: And that is all just the physical. This is much more than the physical: the whole physical world is like nothing.

blocks.text: G-d can take the whole *Ein Sof* and put it into one point, smash it in so tight that you are never going to get it out. So how do we get it out?

phrases.en: it's known,
the truth is,
that a point and a line are not two opposites.

phrases.he: שהרי הקו נמשך מן הנקודה, ומחיבור נקודות יחד נעשה קו כו'.

blocks.text: Now comes the answer, or the introduction to it. It is known that in truth a point and a line, the *reshimu* and the *Kav*, are not two opposites, for the line is drawn from the point: from points joined together a line is made. How do you make a line? You take a point, put another point next to it, and another next to that, point after point, and voila, they make a line. "Ever learned geometry?" A line is defined as a series of points.

blocks.title: The teacher breaks "math" into points
blocks.text: Take the teacher who walks in and writes "math" on the board. If he had stopped there, they would never figure it out. But then he breaks that point up into a bunch of points: after it he writes arithmetic, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, calculus, more advanced stuff. They still do not know what anything is, but now they see there is more than one part to math. Then he breaks arithmetic into addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and breaks those up further: addition of whole numbers, of fractions, decimals, negatives. "Okay, so now today we're going to just focus on one of these little sub-points: addition of whole numbers within arithmetic, within math." And he breaks that into a bunch of examples, 1 and 1 is 2, 2 and 2 is 4, 4 and 4 is 8; each example is one point within the general point. He is still just giving them points, but eventually they have enough points to connect the dots and read between the lines, and they see the whole picture: they catch what you are trying to say.

The same with words. Each word is a point. How can you ever make a person understand by speaking to him, or from a book? Each word alone is a total point, with no intellect to be seen in it, like the word "math": how are you supposed to know what it means? But with the context of a few points, your mind reads between the lines, connects the dots and makes a line out of them. For really you cannot make a line out of points.

blocks.title: In parentheses: a point has no dimensions
blocks.text: "In parentheses", and if you are not familiar with a little geometry, just ignore this: a point really has no dimensions. It is zero-dimensional, infinitely small, so no matter how many you put next to each other it is still zero; it will never become a line. You can say a line is made of points, though it is not really; it is a higher thing. You can use points to describe it, but you need something that fills in the gaps. In the same way, when you put a whole bunch of words together they are able to carry an idea. If your whole language was one word, it would not express enough; with a whole bunch of points you can do it.

blocks.title: The dots of a printed picture
blocks.text: When you see a point alone you do not know what to make of it: whether it is up or down, what it is. It is just a point floating in nothing, with no context and no clues. But take a printed picture, at least in certain styles of printing: the whole thing is made of dots, and yet from far away your mind does not see dots. It sees a whole picture, a continuum, because there is enough for you to connect the dots and fill it in. That is how something revealed in points can come out as a line. But that is more advanced: there are really two things, and they come together. "But okay, end of parenthesis."

The basic idea is that if you take a bunch of points and put them together, it makes a line. Take a pen and make point after point, and it will make a line. That is the way it works. "We're not getting into like ultimate definitions of points right now, unless you want to, then you can read the parenthesis."

The general answer, then: a point and a line are not opposites. And he does not say that a line comes from the points themselves; he says that when you connect a bunch of points, you get a line. You need something that connects them.

sections.title: The point is a hiyuli: it does not spread out because it could become anything
sections.summary: The point is to the line as a *hiyuli* (raw potential) is to its spreading out. Like a child's talent for music, clay, bricks, letters, the ground without a seed or the power of intellect, it does not spread out because it is above spreading out and can become anything, not because it is held back.

phrases.he: אך הענין הוא כידוע שהנקודה הוא כמו בחינת ההיולי לגבי הקו
phrases.en: that the *nekuda*, the relationship of the *reshimu* to the *Kav*, is like the relationship of a *hiyuli* to the *hispashtus*.

blocks.text: The answer, as is known: the *nekuda* is like a *hiyuli* (raw potential) compared to the *Kav*. The relationship of the *reshimu* to the *Kav* is like the relationship of a *hiyuli* to its *hispashtus*. About a *hiyuli* it was asked: is it there or is it not there? In a way it seems not to be there.

blocks.title: Mozart's symphonies in a little kid
blocks.text: Take a person's *hiyuli*, his talent for music. When Beethoven or Mozart was a little kid, were all his symphonies there, in his talent for music? On the one hand, they must all have been there, or else where did they come from? They came out from there. On the other hand, if they were all there, why could he not just write them all out? Because they were totally hidden, there in a way that was like not really there at all, not as a *metzius* (an existence), and that is why he had to work to get them to come out. So too with the *Kav* and the *nekuda*, the *reshimu*: even though it is all there, it is totally hidden.
But that it is totally hidden there does not mean it cannot come out from there. It is hidden there because it is the essence, the source of everything.

blocks.title: The ground needs a seed
blocks.text: Like the ground. The ground will not grow without a seed, not because it cannot grow, but because it could grow anything. So it needs something to tell it which one to grow; it needs to be contracted to one particular plant, because it is too infinite. The same with the power of movement, the power of sight and all these things: since they could come out in any way, the reason they are not coming out is not that they cannot, or have nothing to bring out. They are too infinite.

blocks.title: A one-dot caricature
blocks.text: Put a dot on a piece of paper and ask, "Okay, so what is this a picture of? I'm not drawing the whole picture, I'm just drawing one point that's representing the whole picture." Like a caricature: "I like to do caricatures and just do the main defining details, right?" So you draw this one dot: "Okay, there, that's my caricature. Guess who it is." You can't; it is not enough, because this point is still too infinite. The same point could be a picture of anything, depending on where you put the other points. When you put the other points, you can connect the dots, make the lines, fill it all in in your mind and get the picture. That is the idea of a caricature: you do not need to draw everything. But the point itself is infinite, because it can be used for anything. So too compared to the *Kav*: you can make this one point into any line, and the lines into any shape.

phrases.he: וכמו כל בחינת היולי או חומר פשוט
phrases.en: like any *hiyuli* or any simple matter,

phrases.he: שאף על פי שהוא בהעדר ההתפשטות דוקא,
phrases.en: even though it doesn't spread out,
it's not necessary that it can't spread out,
rather it's just, this is the nature of a *hiyuli*,

phrases.he: מפני שהוא למעלה עדיין מבחינת התפשטות
phrases.en: it's still higher than spreading out.
and that's why, since it's still the essence, it doesn't go down from its essential state.

blocks.text: Like any *hiyuli* or simple matter: even though it does not spread out, that is not necessarily because it cannot. It is just the nature of a *hiyuli*: it is still higher than spreading out.

blocks.title: Clay, bricks and letters
blocks.text: Say you are going to make things out of clay. What is in the clay? In a way, nothing. But the reason nothing is there is not that you cannot make something out of it; it is that you can make anything out of it. And this is the point, "no pun intended": even once you make something out of it, the clay stays just clay. It does not really change, because it is the essence the thing is made of, the same no matter what. The same with bricks: build a building out of them and the bricks do not change, because they are the basic essential unit. The shape you put them in changed, but they are the same bricks; take it apart and you can use them for something else.

blocks.title: The same letters, a different book
blocks.text: The same with letters. Make them into a book, and the same letters can be rearranged in a different order into a different book, because the letters stay on the level of the essential point, and so they can still become anything. Put bricks in one order and it makes a house, in another a barn, in another a wall; put words in one order and it makes one book, in another a different book. The letters stay the same. That you see no intellect in them is not because they cannot express ideas; it is because they are the essential building block, which can express any idea. They always stay that essence, and whether it is revealed like this or like that comes only from the order they are put in.

In the same way, G-d put His whole *etzem* into the *reshimu*. If you want to bring out just this one *hispashtus* from it, you say, "What do you mean? G-d could do anything!" He could bring out any *hishtalshelus*: from the side of the *reshimu*, it is all there. But when He made a number of points in a certain way, we start to connect the dots, and it reveals itself in a certain way. The points stay points, but the light is revealed again only within the imaginary lines that connect the dots, so it reveals only a certain thing. And that is why, **since it's still the essence, it doesn't go down from its essential state**.

phrases.he: וכמו היולי של חיות החי בגלוי,
phrases.en: like the *hiyuli* of the lifeforce, like the consciousness of a living thing,
the way it's still included in the essence,
that it doesn't spread out to enliven, nor to be any consciousness.
like the *hiyuli* of movement, the way it's in the essence
before it spreads out to move.
like the power of growth,
before it grows something.
or like the power of the intellect,
before it spreads out to intellectualize, to come up with ideas.
so too, there are many other examples of this type of *hiyulim*.

blocks.text: Like the *hiyuli* of the lifeforce, the consciousness of a living thing, as it is still included in the essence and does not spread out to enliven. That your essential power of consciousness, as it is in your soul, does not come out to seeing or hearing or any kind of lifeforce is not because it cannot. It is because that is the essence, and it is always there: that you are just alive. That is always there, the basic essence of it.
Like the *hiyuli* of the power of movement, as it is in the essence before it spreads out to move: that it is not moving is not because you cannot move. It is because you can move in any way.

blocks.title: Dirt without a seed
blocks.text: Or the power of growth before it grows something: it is not that it cannot grow. "I want to grow an apple tree. So I'm going to go get me some dirt, and I'm going to grow me an apple tree." He gets dirt, and he waits and waits, and nothing grows, not even weeds. He is all disappointed and does not know why: the other guy had his dirt and all his apple trees were growing, and "I took the same dirt from that same place." Yes, because you have to have a seed. "Why do I need a seed, if it can grow it?" Because it is not going to know what to grow. It is not that the dirt cannot grow. "Oh, so then I just need the seed, great, I'll take the seed, I don't need the dirt." No, because the dirt is really what grows it, not the seed. The seed just tells it how to grow.

Or the power of the intellect before it spreads out to come up with ideas. He could understand anything; that he is not coming up with any ideas now is not because he cannot. He is just not bringing it out into a particular idea, because he could bring out anything, according to his ability, if he is a genius or whatever he is. And there are many other examples of this kind of *hiyuli*: any essence is like this. Music, dancing, any talent at all is like that.

phrases.en: it's understood,
this lack of *hispashtus*,
is not called a true *tzimtzum*,
from itself.
on the contrary,

phrases.he: הרי הוא כח ההיולי העצמי שממנו נמצא הכל בהתגלות והתפשטות
phrases.en: it is the essential *hiyuli* from which everything is found and spreads out.

blocks.text: So it is understood that this lack of *hispashtus* is not called a true *tzimtzum*, from its own side. It is not being held back. The ground, for example, is not trying not to grow anything: "No, I'm not going to grow." **On the contrary**, **it is the essential hiyuli from which everything is found and spreads out**. The ground is saying, "Here, I'll grow anything, I'll grow everything. Just tell me what, I'm ready, whatever you want. Tell me, I'll do it."

sections.title: So too the point and the line: the student who absorbs before he teaches
sections.summary: The point does not spread out only because the whole essence is in it, and the very fact that it is a point shows this. Like a good student who makes himself a point while he absorbs and will not talk in class, it is from this contraction that all the teaching comes afterwards.

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא יובן בבחינת נקודה לגבי הקו
phrases.en: so too, the *nekuda* compared to the *Kav*.

phrases.he: שהעדר התפשטותה הוא רק מצד היותה בבחינת העצמיות שלמעלה מבחינת ההתפשטות עדיין
phrases.en: the only reason that the *reshimu*, the *nekuda*, is not spreading out is because it's still the essence that's higher than spreading out.

phrases.he: והגם שבאה על ידי צמצום הכל,
phrases.en: even though the *nekuda* is made from everything being contracted,

phrases.he: עד שלא נשאר רק כנקודה א' כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: until it's only left like one point, and there's no revelation,

phrases.he: אך הרי זה עצמו מורה שכל בחינת העצמיות כלול בה
phrases.en: The very fact that it's a point shows that the whole essence is there.
and therefore,
it's not coming out to be revealed below,

blocks.text: So too the *nekuda* compared to the *Kav*. The whole power of the Essence is put in there, ready to bring out any *hishtalshelus*; G-d just has to pick which one to bring out, and that is the idea of the *Kav*. It is not that nothing can come out of the *reshimu*. It is true that in the *reshimu* it is totally hidden, but as soon as you put some more dots there, it will reveal different things according to the way you put the dots. The way the *Kav* goes is the way it will reveal.

The only reason the *nekuda* does not spread out is that it is still the essence, higher than spreading out: the essence of everything that could ever come out from this line. And even though the *nekuda* came from everything being contracted, until only one point was left and there was no revelation, that itself shows that the whole essence is included in it. **The very fact that it's a point shows that the whole essence is there**.

Why? Because everything is there, that is why it does not come out to be revealed below: it is not being revealed into one particular thing. Like the ground that can grow everything, and so is not revealed in any particular plant. "Yeah, well we're not talking about that kind of a point." The point here is the one in the *mashal* he is about to give.

phrases.en: like the *mashal* of a student,
sitting before his teacher,
that when he's trying to absorb the teaching of the teacher,

phrases.he: ונעשה כנקודה בצמצום כל עצמותו כו',
phrases.en: where he makes himself like a point, totally focusing his whole being,
he will not spit out,
like, let's say, to teach to somebody else, spreading out.
however,
after he receives from the teacher,
the opposite,
This very *tzimtzum*, this very fact that he was so focused

phrases.he: הוא שנמשך ממנו כל ההשפעה והתפשטות לזולתו כו'

phrases.en: as explained elsewhere.

blocks.title: The good student who says "Not now"
blocks.text: Like a student sitting before his teacher: while he is busy absorbing, he makes himself like a point, with his whole being contracted, and he will not spit out anything to give to someone else. In other words, the good student, the one who can help you with your homework, who will be a teacher and be able to explain it to you later: if you come to him in class while he is listening to the teacher, he will not talk to you at all. Say you missed the last point: "Hey, what did the teacher just say?" "Not now, not now." "Why not? If the whole thing is he wants to be able to teach it and understand it, why won't he do it?" Because right now he is trying to absorb it.

That is why he is a good student: when he listens, he is totally focused. Some people say, for this reason, that it is better not to take notes: listen during class, and take notes after class. If you spend class taking notes, you are not listening fully, not putting your whole self into listening, so you are not really absorbing it properly, because that is already spitting out. A student cannot be spitting out while he is absorbing, or he will not absorb: it shows he is not putting his whole essence into it, not totally focusing on what the teacher is saying.

blocks.title: Focused like a point
blocks.text: To have your attention focused on one point, you cannot be looking anywhere else or thinking about anything else: not looking out the window, not thinking about playing baseball outside. You have to be totally right there, focused like a point. Somebody could say, "Oh look, he's being so mean, he doesn't want to teach anybody." No: he wants to teach everybody, and that is why he makes himself like a point, so that he will be able to explain it afterwards.

blocks.title: The teacher who stops to think
blocks.text: Or the teacher himself, in the *mashal* the Rebbe gives: when he gets a new idea and thinks about it, he stops teaching for a second. He goes up to the idea and makes himself like a point, and stops explaining. But he does it so that he can bring it down to them afterwards, so that he will grasp it and be able to explain it to them, because he wants to explain it to them. The teacher is not contracting himself to hide from the students. He contracts himself up to the idea so that he can get it and bring it down to them, because he really wants to give to them.

The Rebbe says the same thing of the Frierdiker Rebbe: he is going up, and in a way is hidden from us, but that itself is a *gilui*. It shows how much he cares, that he is thinking about the students, because he is going up and stopping in order to get them this. So too he is going to bring down the *gilui* of *Moshiach*.

However, after he receives from the teacher, the opposite: from this very *tzimtzum*, the very fact that he was so focused, would not talk to anybody in class and would not even think for himself about what he was being told, comes all his giving and spreading out to others.

When you are listening to a teacher, you are not supposed to think about what he is saying; you are just supposed to absorb it. Do not try to figure out how it fits with other things, or interpret it. Take it in in its pure state and retain the facts as he says them; afterwards you will sort it out and see how it fits with other things. Like when somebody is telling you a story: you just want to picture the story and follow it. That is the best way to learn. Afterwards you think about it, interpret it and work on it on your own. A person who learns like that is afterwards a very good teacher, able to really explain it to somebody else, and if you listen, it really sticks with you. As explained elsewhere.

phrases.en: from all this understood,

phrases.he: שהקו הנמשך מן הנקודה הוא רק כמו בחינת התפשטות מן היולי העצמי
phrases.en: the line that comes out from the point, that relationship is like the spreading out from a *hiyuli*.

blocks.text: From all this it is understood that the line drawn from the point is only like the spreading out from an essential *hiyuli*. The *nekuda* stays hidden, but that does not stop the revelation; on the contrary, it is its source. The *reshimu* is truly a *nekuda*, higher than ever being revealed, and it is never totally revealed, because it is infinite and can reveal anything, while the *Kav* reveals only one *hishtalshelus*. Nevertheless the *reshimu* is the source of the *Kav*, and everything in the *hishtalshelus* comes out from the *reshimu* through the *Kav*. Yet the whole *reshimu* is never revealed.

But that the whole *reshimu* is not revealed does not stop things from being revealed from it: you can reveal anything you want from it. It just will not be totally revealed, because it is essentially a *hiyuli*, and it is impossible to reveal the whole thing. "I mean, G-d could do it," but you cannot do it one line at a time, because it is infinite. So it is never fully revealed: it is too big of a zero.

As they say: a guy keeps saying, "I'm a nothing, I'm a nothing," and another guy says, "Look who thinks he's a nothing. I'm a bigger nothing." So the *reshimu* is a nothing, but it is a bigger nothing than our whole world.

sections.title: The short line: a hiyuli for length and breadth that makes an up and a down
sections.summary: As the point is a *hiyuli* for the line, so the short line is a *hiyuli* for the length and breadth of an area. It explains nothing in particular; it only makes an up and a down, a giver and a receiver, like the order of subjects in school, and that, says *Etz Chaim*, is its whole purpose.

phrases.en: however,
why is the *Kav* revealed in a way of like a short line?
it's explained elsewhere,

phrases.he: שכמו שהנקודה בחינת היולי לגבי הקו,
phrases.en: just like the point of the *reshimu* is a *hiyuli* compared to the *Kav*,

phrases.he: כך הקו בחינת היולי לבחינת אורך ורוחב דשטח
phrases.en: So too, a line is a *hiyuli* for a length and a width.

blocks.text: Now another point, "a new paragraph". Why is the *Kav* drawn as a *kav katzar* (a short line)? What does it mean that it is a short line? It is explained elsewhere: just as the point of the *reshimu* is a *hiyuli* compared to the *Kav*, so the line is a *hiyuli* for the length and breadth of a *shetach* (an area). Put a bunch of points together and you make a line; put a bunch of lines together and you can draw all kinds of neat little shapes. But the line is the basic building block: the same line can draw any shape, done over and over in different ways, just as the line is the same point done over and over. So in the big picture the line is kind of like a point.

What is the difference between a line and a point? A point has no context whatsoever: no dimensions, no up, no down, no right or left. You do not know what it is; it is just there. A line already shows a direction, that it is going a certain way, so it already has the idea of an up and a down. You may not know which way it points, since the paper could be turned, but you already see a direction, a polarity, ends going opposite ways. That is an essential difference between it and a point, and that is what is going to be said: the whole *inyan* (matter) of the line is to make an up and a down.

That is why the kabbalists made an analogy of the *Kav* to a line. It is not really a line; they use the *mashal* of a line because of this relationship of a point and a line. "It's not like the upstairs is lines and points and, you know, G-d's like drawing with a compass and a pencil, you know what I mean?" Nor is it physical light coming down in a line. It is not a physical thing at all; it is a *mashal*. Everything eventually has to be translated into something we know, into how it is in us.

phrases.en: it's known,
the line,

phrases.he: הגם שהוא בא בבחינת המשכה והתפשטות מלמעלה למטה,
phrases.en: even though a line is already spreading out from up to down, it's already drawn out,

phrases.he: אבל אינו ענין פרטית אופן המשכה כלל
phrases.en: It's not a particular way of *hamshacha*,

phrases.he: רק מה שנמשך האור מלמעלה למטה בלבד
phrases.en: it's just the idea of light of going from up to down.

blocks.text: It is known that the line, even though it already spreads out from above to below and is already drawn out, is not any particular way of *hamshacha* (drawing down) at all. It is only the idea of the light going from up to down. What does that mean?

blocks.title: The order of subjects in school
blocks.text: Say the teacher takes the point of math he wrote on the board and, as was said before, breaks it up into arithmetic, algebra, geometry and calculus, and then breaks arithmetic into addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. He keeps breaking it up.

blocks.title: Five oranges and one fishy
blocks.text: That breaking up of the point of math into a hierarchy of more basic ideas: "now my wife's going to teach today; she's starting to teach math and ABCs to the little kids at the *cheder* here, right?" She is going to teach them how to add. You start from the beginning, from adding five and eight, or even before that: "I don't even know what they're doing. I think they're just like counting things and knowing what number it is." They have a picture of five oranges, and underneath it says four, five, six, and they have to circle the right one. They have to learn how to count; that is the basic thing. Then they learn how to add: one fishy and one fishy equals two fishies. Those are the basic things, and later come the more advanced things.

sensitivity.reason: Names his wife's teaching job at the local school.
sensitivity.publishable: That breaking up of the point of math into a hierarchy of more basic ideas: think of a teacher who is starting to teach math to the little kids. She is going to teach them how to add. You start from the beginning, from adding five and eight, or even before that: just counting things and knowing what number it is. They have a picture of five oranges, and underneath it says four, five, six, and they have to circle the right one. They have to learn how to count; that is the basic thing. Then they learn how to add: one fishy and one fishy equals two fishies. Those are the basic things, and later come the more advanced things.

blocks.text: So there is already a whole hierarchy of up and down. That is the idea of a line broken out of a point. But the line is still not a particular explanation of any of those subjects. It just breaks up math so that you can evaluate what level a person is on and know which subject to teach him, which grade he is in. That the grades are divided by subject, with a class plan for each year, just tells you what to teach: if you are here on the line, now we will talk about this part of math. It is not yet an actual explanation of anything. The actual explanation is like the *shetach* that comes out from the line.

But first you have to break the point up into a line, because to somebody who really knows math, arithmetic is not really more basic than calculus; they are all the same. To make it simple, you decide that this will be the beginning and this the end, you put it in an order, and you start from a certain place.

The same is said about *Chassidus*. *Chassidus* is really in the way of circles: it has no beginning and no end; it is all really one point. So how can you explain it? You cannot really explain it; you have to get it. Nevertheless it has to be learned in an orderly way, and the advice is that the first thing to learn is the *seder hishtalshelus* (the chain of descending worlds) as it is explained in *Shaar HaYichud* (the Gate of Unity). That is in a letter from the Frierdiker Rebbe, who quotes the Rebbe Rashab in the name of the *Rebbe Maharash* (the fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe).

So it is a tradition of the Chabad Rebbeim: even though *Chassidus* has no beginning and no end, and it seems impossible ever to jump in and start understanding it, there is a way in, and that is the only book written in a line, *Shaar HaYichud*. It goes straight from up to down. All the other books do not; they are somewhere in the middle, and you are floating, a point in the middle of nowhere with no context to figure out what they are talking about. The real *kavana* (intention) is to learn the other books and get the *etzem*, but to get it you first have to do this line and learn the *seder hishtalshelus* like this, from up to down.

phrases.he: שעל ידי זה נמצא בחינת מעלה ומטה מהמשפיע אל המקבל
phrases.en: This creates the idea of up and down from the *mashpia* to the *mekabel*,
but in the *hiyuli* of the point,

phrases.he: אין בו מעלה ומטה, ראש תוך וסוף כו' כידוע
phrases.en: there's no up, down, beginning, middle, or end.
this is what it says in *Etz Chaim*,

phrases.he: דכל עיקר הארת הקו אינו רק להיות בחינת מעלה ומטה כמו שיתבאר)
phrases.en: The whole purpose of the line is to create the idea of up and down.

blocks.title: The ladder up to the diploma
blocks.text: This makes an up and a down from the *mashpia* (the giver) to the *mekabel* (the receiver): the teacher is the top and the student is the bottom, and you have to make a ladder between them. First you learn this, then you learn that, and as you grow you get closer and closer until you graduate, and they give you a diploma and say, now you can be a teacher. That is a line from up to down. That is all the idea of the *Kav* is: making the system of measurement.

But in the *hiyuli* of the point it is not so. The line is also a *hiyuli*, but at least it has an up and a down. With this system it is a *hiyuli* for any class plan: in any class you are going to teach, on any day of it, you will know what to teach based on where they are in the subject, what we will teach today and what tomorrow. As soon as we learn this, we will learn that. It can come out in infinite ways, depending on where they are up to. And each of those things can be explained in different ways and with different examples; once you take it off into a width, each teacher can explain it differently, and the class can go differently.

But the line stays the same, and it has an up and a down. All classes and all teachers are never the same, no two years alike, even with the same teacher, and surely not with two different teachers teaching the same thing. Nevertheless everybody goes through the same hierarchy of subjects: addition, then subtraction, then multiplication, then division; then algebra, geometry, trigonometry, calculus. It is always the same order. Each thing can be brought out in different ways, which is like a width, but the basic line of how you climb the ladder of math is the same. "I mean I'm not saying it has to be done totally that way," but say there is a standard, "which there pretty much is": you keep that the same and still have infinite different ways it comes out.

You could change the point too: go to science class, and the whole point is different. Instead of math he writes "science" on the board, and it is a different class, with its own line. But in the line you at least know which grade you are in and which class to go to. Come in the middle of the year, behind the class, and they are already farther up the line: you know where you are supposed to go. There is an up and a down.

But in the *hiyuli* of the point **there's no up, down, beginning, middle, or end**. So you walk in and say, "Listen guys, math, you just got to get it. Either you got it or you don't. I got it and you don't, there's nothing you could do about it." You cannot teach it, because it is an all-or-nothing thing. "How am I supposed to teach something like that?" At that level it is not even something you can discuss teaching to somebody else.

With a line, you have not actually taught anyone yet, but you are already discussing the idea; you have already thought of a student. That is the whole point of the *Kav*: you did not teach yet, but you thought there is going to be a student and you are going to have to bring it down. And you are ready to bring it down to any student, not to a particular one; you have your system for figuring out what to teach ready. In the point you are not yet ready to bring it out to anybody, because to bring it out you have to go through this whole process of *tzimtzum* to make it teachable. The way you have it, "I just got it, I know it. It's all one point by me, I have the whole thing, and I can't express it to you. It just is." How do you add? "You do it, come on. Everybody knows that, I just do it." You cannot tell that to a kid; he will not get it.

And this is what *Etz Chaim* says: the whole point of the shining of the *Kav* is only to make an up and a down, as will be explained. **The whole purpose of the line is to create the idea of up and down**.

sections.title: One measuring rod for the whole house, three lines for every letter
sections.summary: You do not buy a stick for every length: one ruler, the smallest unit, measures out any house, and three lines make an A, an N or a Y. So the short line, which only makes up and down, is a *hiyuli* for every measure and every letter.

phrases.en: like a measuring rod

phrases.he: שאינו בא בגדר שטח הבנין עצמו, לאורך ורוחב
רק שבו מודד כל מדידת אורך וכל מדידת רוחב
phrases.en: but with the same measuring stick you measure every length and every width.

phrases.he: והוא עצמו רק כמו קו הקצר
phrases.en: and all it is is a little line, little stick,

phrases.he: שכולל כל אופני מדידות של אורך ורוחב כו'
phrases.en: and in this stick is hidden all possible combinations of lengths and widths,

blocks.title: A 150-foot measuring stick
blocks.text: Like the measuring rod of a building, which does not come within the area of the building itself, its length and breadth. Say you want to build a house 150 feet this way by 100 feet that way, three stories high, "I don't know, how tall is that, let's say 45 feet," and each room a different size, this one 10 by 12, this one 8 by 6, and then the doorway, the trim, the windows: all these different measurements. So what do you do? Go to the measuring stick store and buy yourself a 150-foot measuring stick for one side, a 100-foot one for the other, and for each room a 10-foot one, a 12-foot one, a 6-foot one? "No, that's ridiculous." You get one measuring thing and use it for the whole thing.

blocks.title: One ruler for the whole house
blocks.text: You do not buy one for each size. You buy one yardstick, or one ruler. To measure 100 feet you put the ruler down, and again, and again, until you have measured out 100 feet; and if it has inches marked off on it, you can measure inches too. All you need is the smallest unit you are ever going to need to measure, and once you have that, you multiply it over and over. That is the idea of the *Kav*: all it has to do is create the idea of up and down. Once the smallest unit of up and down is made, you can measure out any *shetach* you want. It is already a *hiyuli* for measuring out anything, in any direction, of any size. You just create your standard of measurement and multiply it; you do not need a separate one for each thing.

With the same measuring stick you measure every length and every width, doing it over and over. "It's a magic *hiyuli* measuring rod. You know, people say we don't have magic stuff. We have magic *hiyuli* measuring sticks that can measure out any length." It is kind of like a genie in a bottle: buy this ruler and it will measure out any length you want. Amazing: *hiyuli* powers.

And it itself is only a short line, a little stick, and hidden in this stick are all possible combinations of lengths and widths, all of them. The idea of creating the *Kav* is just to create a way to measure, a system for what is up and down and right and left, and once that system is there, you can measure out anything. But you did not actually measure anything out yet. It is not an actual *hamshacha*: you did not measure out a certain length and width; you only created the ability to measure them. It is still *hiyuli*, still infinite.

blocks.title: The lesson plan and the teacher
blocks.text: In the math classroom, the lesson plan is the line you use to measure up a student, to figure out what level he is on and how to teach him. But a teacher also has the central ability to do that, which he could use for any class, and that is the real line. The real *hiyuli* line is that he can create a system, a hierarchy, for any class, a way to measure up any student and a way to divide it up.

phrases.he: כך ציור הקו בחינת היולי לגבי בחינת שטח האותיות לעשותם באורך ורוחב,
phrases.en: So, too, a line is also *hiyuli* for the *shetach* of letters, to be able to write them in a length and a width.

phrases.he: כמו בחינת קוין שבאות הב' כו'
phrases.en: like the lines in the letter beis,
as explained elsewhere.

blocks.title: Three lines make an A
blocks.text: So too the drawing of the line is a *hiyuli* for the *shetach* of the letters, to make them in length and breadth. Take a little kid: "she's teaching them how to write the ABCs, my wife's teaching them, right?" "Kids, do you know how to write the ABCs?" "No." "Well, can you make a line?" "Yeah." "Well, if you can make a line, then you can make the ABCs. Look, I'll show you. Make a line here like that, and then make another one here like that, and make another one here like that, and now you have an A." Three lines, that is all you have to do. Take the same three and put them a different way, and you have an N; another way, and you have a Y. "You know, it's magic. Magic lines." That is the *Kav*: the *Kav* is a *hiyuli* to make any letters.

blocks.text: Now the *mashal* here: **like the lines in the letter beis**. It is three lines, and you can take those same three lines and put them together into the English letter N. As explained elsewhere.

sections.title: The kav hamida: the first line, short, carrying the Essence to the receivers
sections.summary: The beginning of the line goes out the smallest possible amount, only to make up and down, and so it is the *kav hamida*, the standard every measure is made from. Yet it carries all that was hidden in the point, the real light of the Essence of the giver, measured to the receivers.

phrases.en: and based on this,

phrases.he: גם ראשית המשכת הקו מן הנקודה,
phrases.en: even the first *hamshacha* of the *Kav* from the *nekuda*, coming out from the *reshimu*,

phrases.he: הגם שהוא בא בבחינת התפשטות והמשכה,
phrases.en: even though it's already *hispashtus* and *hamshacha* compared to the *Kav*,

phrases.he: אבל הוא בחינת המשכה היולית עדיין,
phrases.en: this is a *hiyuli* *hamshacha*,

phrases.he: לכלול כמה פרטי אופני המשכות לאורך ורוחב במדה
phrases.en: to include many different particular ways of bringing out to length and width in the actual *midda*,
that's why it's called the measuring line,

blocks.text: Based on this, even the first drawing of the *Kav* from the *nekuda*, coming out from the *reshimu*, is called the *reshis hakav* (the beginning of the line): this little *hiyuli* *Kav*. All it does is go from up to down. It did not go all the way out to make the whole lesson plan. All G-d did was take the line and make it go from up to down, which means it went out the smallest possible amount, infinitely small. As soon as it went out at all, it stopped, because it had created the idea of up and down.

That is all that needed to be done. Once you have the smallest possible thing, you have a context of an up and a down, and that is all we wanted. Then the concept of up and down, before and after, is reapplied over and over in all different directions and ways, to make all the different things. That is the *reshis hakav*, the *hiyuli* for all the different *hishtalshelus* and everything that comes out: just making things relate to each other in different ways, "this one's upper, and this one's lower, and this one's righter, and this one's lefter." It gives the potential for the whole *hishtalshelus*: to take the *nekuda*, break it up in all different possible ways and bring it out in all different things.

So this *reshis hakav*, even though it is already *hispashtus* and *hamshacha*, is a *hiyuli* *hamshacha*, to include many particular ways of drawing out to length and breadth in the actual *midda* (measure), like the ruler you can measure out all different kinds of houses with. So too this can bring out anything from the *Kav*.

That is why it is called the *kav hamida* (the line of measure): all it is is the standard of measurement, just the idea of making up and down. Once you have the smallest unit of up and down, you do that over and over again, and you can make anything you want and measure whatever you want.

phrases.en: and this is indicated by its shape,
it's essentially short,
it just goes from up to down.

phrases.he: אבל הוא כולל בהמשכתו על כל פנים כל מה שיש בהעלם ההיולי דנקודה כו',
phrases.en: but in this *hamshacha*, it includes, in a hidden way, everything that was hidden in the *nekuda*.
just that now it's coming out down.

blocks.title: An anything stick
blocks.text: Its shape shows it: **it's essentially short**, and **it just goes from up to down**. As soon as it went down, it stopped, because all that was needed was to make it the standard of measurement. As was said, to measure anything you have to have the smallest one. With only a foot stick you can measure anything in pieces of a foot: 1 foot, 2 feet, 3 feet, 100 feet. But to measure a foot and a half you need a half-foot stick; to measure inches you need inch sticks; millimeters, millimeter sticks. And to be able to measure anything, you need an anything stick, which is infinitely small. All it is is an anything; it is just a something. "A something can measure anything as long as it's only a something." If it is anything more than a something, it cannot measure anything. So to be a *hiyuli* for measuring anything, it has to be just from up to down.

Yet in its drawing down it includes, in a hidden way, everything that was hidden in the *hiyuli* of the *nekuda*: it can bring out everything in the *nekuda* in all different ways. Only now it comes out downward. Like the teacher who is explaining: he is bringing over the whole thing, but in a way that measures it out and brings it to the level of the student.

phrases.he: והוא בא מכח אור העצמי הנעלם שבעצמות המשפיע שלפני צמצומו בנקודה א'

phrases.en: only that it's coming in a measured way, though. It's coming in just a line.
not coming the way that it's in the *mashpia*.

phrases.he: שהוא בהרחבת הערך של העצמות ממש
phrases.en: and that in the *mashpia*, it's totally big like the *Atzmus*.

blocks.title: The children learn the teacher's own math
blocks.text: It comes from the power of the hidden essential light in the essence of the *mashpia*, from before its contraction into one point. The teacher first decided he is going to teach math: that is the *nekuda*. Then he readies his *Kav* to measure up the students and figure out how to explain it to them on their level. But the explanations he gives are the actual math as the teacher knows it. They are actually getting math, in a very small, short, little way, but it is the actual thing from before the *tzimtzum*: just a little of it, very limited, but actually some of the knowledge he had. He knows 1 and 1 is 2; that is actually what he knows. So what comes out from the *Kav* is actually from before the *tzimtzum*. It is extracting what was originally put in there, reconstituting it, like the *Gemara* coming out of the *Mishna* again.

Only it comes by way of a line, in a measured way, and not as it is in the essence of the *mashpia*. In the *mashpia* it is infinite, as broad as the *Atzmus* (G-d's essence) itself; here it comes out in a very thin, little way.

phrases.he: ובקו זה הנה אור העצמות בא לפי ערך המקבלים לבד
phrases.en: but in this line, it's coming only according to the *mekablim*.
nevertheless,

phrases.he: הרי יש בו מעין ודוגמת אור העצמות הנעלם בנקודה כו',
phrases.en: it does have a *maayan* and *dugma* of what was hidden in the *nekuda*,
it's just coming in a way to be brought down below,
therefore it's in the line, that it's measured and very small,

phrases.he: והוא בחינת היולי לכל אור ושפע המקבלים כו' ודי למבין:
phrases.en: And this line is a *hiyuli* for everything that comes out to the *mekablim*.

blocks.text: In this line the light of the *Atzmus* comes only according to the measure of the receivers. If they are very little, it comes in a very little way, measured to come down to their level. If they are first graders, it is going to be "very stupid, little things compared to him."

Nevertheless it has a *maayan* (a wellspring) and *dugma* (a likeness) of the light of the *Atzmus* hidden in the *nekuda*, because it is still really math: he is still explaining the same thing, and they are actually understanding something that he understands. Only it comes by way of drawing down below.

That is why it comes in the form of a line: measured and very small. The line shows that it is a finite, very thin and measured revelation; that is what it represents. And, as will be said later: if they really were on his level, he would just talk straight, the way he knows it, and it would not be hidden at all. He could bring out the whole light from the *Kav* again if he wanted to, the whole light from before the *tzimtzum*.

And the line is a *hiyuli* for all the light and flow of the receivers: the ability to limit the light and bring it out to them according to their level, in any way that will be appropriate. That is the general story of the *Kav*, and after this more particular things will be explained.

reviewQuestions.question: Why is the tzimtzum itself no obstacle to a revelation coming out of the reshimu, and what would a tzimtzum kipshuto look like?
Why does the point still seem to be a true tzimtzum, and what does a teacher who writes "math" on the board and walks out show?
Why will the ground not grow without a seed, and what does that teach about a hiyuli?
Why will a good student not answer your question in class, and what comes from his being a point?
What is the difference between a point and a line, and what is the whole purpose of the Kav?
Why is the beginning of the line short, and why is it called the kav hamida?

notes.text: No student is heard, but in a few places he seems to answer someone: 35 w1314 ("Right, you have partial and complete tzimtzum in that way, that's like a kipshuto, yeah"), 36 w360 ("Right, exactly."), 37 w59 ("You need something connects them with, yeah"), 37 w2184 ("Yeah, well we're not talking about that kind of a point") and 35 w2054-2080 on the dot and the reshimu. With no question audible, these are kept in his voice and no question block is written.

Some phrases cite his rendering inside the explanation rather than right after the reading: line 3 (35 w174-233), line 27 (37 w2141-2151) and line 31's first phrase (38 w26-36). Line 9's second half (זהו עיקר סיבת כל גלוי ההשפעה) has no English: what follows the reading (35 w1010-1022, "All the lights in the hishtalshelus are all coming out from the reshimu") is his explanation, not a rendering of those words.

Line 12: he reads the whole line, translates its second half first ("the Kav is the opposite of this", 36 w1154-1160) and then asks "How does the Kav come out from the reshimu?" (w1168-1176), so the phrase audio is out of order.

Line 43: the English of the phrases from "even though it's already hispashtus" on comes from his second reading (39 w1341-1404). There he says "compared to the Kav" where the sense seems to be compared to the point; the phrase keeps his words.
Lines 5-6: he reads line 6's opening ("like the form of a yud") at the end of his sentence on line 5 (35 w393-401), before the alignment mark for line 6.

The remark on the Frierdiker Rebbe (37 w2757-2827), that his going up is itself a revelation and that he is going to bring down the revelation of Moshiach, is given as a mashal of "the Rebbe" and left unflagged as a Chabad teaching; a reviewer for the public edition may want to look at it.

Sources reported as he gave them: Rabbi Chaim Vital's introduction to Etz Chaim on why the Zohar was written hidden (36 w873-1134), and a letter of the Frierdiker Rebbe quoting the Rebbe Rashab in the name of the Rebbe Maharash, that Shaar HaYichud is the way into Chassidus (38 w1658-1681). Neither is checked.
